headline: Jeffries nominated for Speaker as MORE Act reaches 77 sponsors
dek: House Democrats chose Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker on 18 November; the descheduling bill he once co-sponsored gained its 77th sponsor on 20 November.
key_points: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries of New York for Speaker on 18 November by 251 votes to 11 in a closed-door ballot, the Associated Press reported, as relayed by Cannabis Business Times.
Jeffries co-sponsored the MORE Act when the House passed it in 2020 and 2022, but has not signed the 2023 or 2025 versions since becoming minority leader.
Rep. Valerie Foushee of North Carolina joined the current MORE Act, H.R. 5068, on 20 November, taking it to 77 sponsors, The Marijuana Herald reported.
Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats in January, four short of the 60 needed to end a filibuster, so any cannabis bill still needs Republican votes or a filibuster-proof vehicle.
body: The politician who will decide which bills reach the House floor next year is on record wanting to end federal cannabis prohibition. House Democrats nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York for Speaker on Wednesday 18 November. He won a closed-door vote 251 to 11, according to the Associated Press as relayed by Cannabis Business Times. The full House votes in January, when the new Congress is sworn in.

Two days later the main descheduling bill in the House picked up another name. Rep. Valerie Foushee, a North Carolina Democrat, signed on to the Marijuana Opportunity Reinvestment and Expungement (MORE) Act on Friday 20 November, The Marijuana Herald reported. She is the bill's 77th sponsor and the second to join this month, after Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona on 10 November.
## What Jeffries has said and done

Jeffries was one of five initial co-sponsors of the MORE Act in 2021, Cannabis Business Times reports. He also co-sponsored the earlier version that passed the House 228 to 164 in 2020. When the House passed the bill again in 2022, by 220 to 204, he spoke for it on the floor and tied the growth of the US prison population to drug enforcement, including marijuana possession.

"It's time to end the federal cannabis prohibition," he said in that 2022 speech, according to the outlet. He also called for descheduling and for investment in the communities most affected by enforcement.

His record since then is more cautious. Jeffries became House minority leader in 2023 and has not co-sponsored the MORE Act in either of its later versions, which Rep. Jerry Nadler of New York introduced in 2023 and 2025. Party leaders often stay off bills they may later have to schedule, so the gap is not proof of a change of mind. It does mean his most recent commitment on descheduling is four years old.

He has kept working on a smaller, bipartisan bill. In 2025 Jeffries and Rep. Dave Joyce, an Ohio Republican, reintroduced the PREPARE Act for the third Congress in a row. It would have the attorney general set up a commission to study how the federal government could regulate cannabis in a way similar to alcohol, with input from state regulators, industry, health experts and justice-reform groups. It legalizes nothing. It is a plan for what happens after legalization.
## Where the MORE Act stands

The current MORE Act is H.R. 5068, introduced by Nadler on 29 August 2025. It would take marijuana out of the Controlled Substances Act altogether, rather than moving it to a lower schedule. It would end federal criminal penalties for possession, manufacturing and distribution, set up expungement and resentencing for some federal convictions, and bring in a federal excise tax that starts at 5% and rises to 8%, The Marijuana Herald reports. The money would go to reinvestment, job training and treatment programmes. The bill would also open Small Business Administration services to cannabis firms.

It has not moved. The bill sits in several House committees and has had no floor vote. Before Ansari signed on 10 November, it had gone almost four months without a new sponsor; the previous one was Rep. Marilyn Strickland of Washington on 13 July.

Our arithmetic puts the support in context. Seventy-seven sponsors is 17.7% of the 435-seat House and 141 short of the 218 needed to pass a bill. Democrats are projected to hold 259 seats next year, Cannabis Business Times reports, after flipping at least 43. The sponsor list would have to nearly triple to match the party's own numbers.
> Seventy-seven names is a marker of intent. The number that matters in January is 218, and after that 60.

There is also a calendar problem. A bill that has not passed when a Congress ends has to be introduced again in the next one. H.R. 5068 belongs to the outgoing Congress, so it will need a new number and a fresh sponsor list in 2027. Names added now are best read as signals from members who will be asked to sign again in January.
## The Senate is still the hard part

The House has passed the MORE Act twice and the Senate has never voted on it. That was true under Republican control in 2020 and under Democratic control in 2022, the outlet notes, because most bills need 60 votes to get past a filibuster.

As we reported on 18 November, Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats in the new Congress. That is four short of 60. A descheduling bill would need at least four Republican senators, or it would have to ride on a budget reconciliation package or another vehicle that cannot be filibustered. We reported on 16 November that the two Democrats competing to lead the Senate differ on cannabis, so the Senate's priorities are not yet set either.

The White House is a third variable. On 6 November we reported an adviser's claim that President Trump would sign a clean descheduling bill. That is a claim about a bill that does not yet exist in the form described.
## What advocates want first

Reform groups are already setting expectations. Morgan Fox, political director of NORML, said after the midterms that Congress, not agencies or courts, should settle the question by descheduling cannabis, Cannabis Business Times reports. He noted that cannabis bills have done better under Democratic control, pointing to the MORE Act and to the SAFE Banking Act, which the House passed seven times between 2019 and 2022.

Banking is the nearer prize for operators. Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Joyce reintroduced the SAFE Banking Act in June 2026 with bipartisan co-sponsors, and it has not advanced in this Congress. Public opinion is not the obstacle: an October 2025 Gallup poll put support for legalization at 64% of US adults, according to the outlet.
## What it means

For operators and investors, the practical change in January is who controls the House floor. A Speaker decides what gets a vote. Jeffries has voted for descheduling twice and co-sponsored it twice, and he has a bipartisan record on preparing for federal regulation. None of that commits him to a date or a bill.

It also does not change the present position. State-licensed medical cannabis is in Schedule III, the wider rescheduling process is unfinished, and adult-use businesses remain outside federal law. A House vote on descheduling would be a statement of the chamber's position. Whether it becomes law depends on the Senate and the president.
## What to watch

Watch the Speaker election when the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027. Watch who reintroduces the MORE Act, how many of the 77 return as original co-sponsors, and whether Jeffries adds his name. Watch committee assignments, since the bill has been referred to several panels. Watch whether House leaders move banking first as a bill that can attract Republican votes. And watch the Senate leadership contest, which will show how much floor time cannabis gets in the other chamber.
